slots.practicalActivity: pip install azure-ai-ml locally and construct a Workspace entity object (Workspace(name="mlw-churn-dev", location="eastus", display_name=...)) without calling Azure, printing its fields to see exactly what a workspace definition requires. Then plan, on paper, a one-workspace-per-project layout for a hypothetical team with 3 ML projects, naming each workspace and listing which of the 4 companion resources (storage account, Key Vault, Application Insights, Container Registry) each would need.
slots.deliverable: A local Python script that builds and prints a Workspace object's fields, plus a written one-workspace-per-project naming plan for 3 hypothetical projects.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's real fingerprinting script locally: write out a conda spec pinned to your actually-installed numpy/pandas/scikit-learn versions, hash it with hashlib.sha256, then change only the scikit-learn version string and confirm the hash changes completely. Separately, construct (no network call) ComputeInstance, AmlCompute, and Environment entity objects locally with idle-shutdown and min_instances=0 settings, printing each to see the required fields.
slots.deliverable: Two printed spec hashes (original and one-version-changed) proving a single pin change produces a different environment fingerprint, plus 3 locally-constructed compute/environment entity objects with their printed configuration.

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the lesson's versioning analogy on your own small CSV: write a describe(name, version, path) function that reads the file, computes a sha256 hash, and reports its row count and type as a JSON data-asset description. Append 2 rows to the file, save it as a new version, and run describe() again, confirming the hash and row count both changed while the original file's description stays reproducible.
slots.deliverable: Two JSON data-asset descriptions (version 1 and version 2) for the same evolving CSV, each with a distinct sha256 hash and row count, proving why overwriting data in place would break reproducibility.

slots.practicalActivity: Turn the chapter's churn-classifier notebook logic into a real argparse script (train.py with --data, --n_estimators, --learning_rate) and run it locally end to end, confirming it prints accuracy and AUC. Run the lesson's command-mimic script that fills in ${{inputs.data}} placeholders and launches train.py as a subprocess. Then write a job.yml in the documented command-job schema, edit it to bump n_estimators and the data version, and use PyYAML plus difflib to produce a 2-line reviewable diff exactly like the lesson's pull-request example.
slots.deliverable: A working train.py run locally with printed accuracy/AUC, the subprocess command-mimic output showing the expanded command line, and a 2-line YAML diff showing a tracked hyperparameter and data-version change.

slots.practicalActivity: Extend your train.py script from the previous slot to write model.joblib and metrics.json to a --model_dir folder, run it locally and confirm both files are saved, exactly as a job would keep its 'outputs'. Then deliberately break it (pass a nonexistent file name) and read the resulting FileNotFoundError traceback the way you would read it from a job's std_log.txt in the studio's Outputs + logs tab.
slots.deliverable: A model_dir folder containing model.joblib and metrics.json from a successful run, plus the captured traceback text from one deliberately broken run.

slots.practicalActivity: Point MLflow at a local file:./mlruns store, run the lesson's churn script 3 times with learning_rate 0.3, 0.1, and 0.03, logging params and metrics by hand, then use mlflow.search_runs to sort all 3 by AUC. Separately run mlflow.sklearn.autolog() on the same pipeline and compare its training_accuracy_score against your own manually-logged test accuracy to see why autolog's numbers can mislead.
slots.deliverable: A sorted mlflow.search_runs table of the 3 manually-logged runs by AUC, plus a side-by-side comparison showing autolog's training-only accuracy versus your real test-set accuracy.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the lesson's hand-rolled AutoML miniature: score logistic regression, k-NN, a decision tree, a random forest, and gradient boosting on the same churn table with 3-fold cross-validated AUC, then rank them. Confirm (or refute) the lesson's finding that the simplest model wins, and write a one-paragraph note on what AutoML's real automatic featurization and early-stopping would add on top of your manual loop.
slots.deliverable: A ranked 5-model AUC table from your own cross-validation loop, plus a short written note on the gap between your manual comparison and real AutoML.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's local sweep: sample 8 random (learning_rate, max_depth) combinations with a log-uniform learning rate, train a GradientBoostingClassifier for each, and log every trial as a nested MLflow run, then read back which trial scored best. Then build the 2-step local pipeline: write data_prep.py (splits data, logs num_rows) and train.py (trains, logs accuracy, saves an MLflow model) as separate scripts, and write a small Python runner that launches each as its own subprocess tied to its own MLflow run, confirming the final accuracy matches a single-script run.
slots.deliverable: A table of all 8 sweep trials with their learning_rate, max_depth, and accuracy, plus console output from the 2-step pipeline runner showing the data_prep num_rows metric and the train step's final accuracy logged as separate MLflow runs.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's Databricks-quickstart workflow locally against a file:./mlruns store: train a GradientBoostingClassifier with mlflow.sklearn.autolog() on, log a manual test_auc metric, reload the model with mlflow.pyfunc.load_model and confirm its predictions exactly match the original model's, then use mlflow.search_runs to find the best run by test_auc.
slots.deliverable: Printed output showing the test AUC, the assertion that the reloaded pyfunc model's predictions match the original, and the best run's id and AUC from search_runs.

slots.practicalActivity: Run a 12-trial local Optuna study tuning n_estimators, learning_rate, and max_depth for a GradientBoostingClassifier, logging each trial as a nested MLflow run and the best trial's AUC via search_runs. Then register 2 model versions locally under one three-level-style name (e.g. "prod.ml_team.churn_model") with input_example-inferred signatures, and use set_registered_model_alias to point a Champion alias first at version 1 and then re-point it at version 2.
slots.deliverable: The Optuna study's best AUC and parameters from search_runs, plus console output confirming the Champion alias correctly re-points from version 1 to version 2.

lessons.title: Feature Engineering at Scale With Spark

slots.practicalActivity: Build the lesson's cutoff-based feature pipeline in pandas on a synthetic orders table: compute orders_30d, spend_30d, and days_since_last strictly from data before a 2025-03-01 cutoff, build the bought_in_march label strictly from data after it, and fit a logistic regression to confirm you get a plausible AUC. Then reproduce the pandas.merge_asof point-in-time join on 3 monthly feature snapshots to prove a later event only ever sees the snapshot that existed at its own timestamp, never a future one.
slots.deliverable: A fitted leakage-safe feature table with its AUC, plus the merge_asof output proving an event on 2025-03-15 received the February snapshot and not the March one.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's local stand-in for a Fabric experiment: fit 2 logistic-regression pipelines with C=0.1 and C=1.0 on synthetic churn data, log each with mlflow.log_param/log_metric and an inferred signature via mlflow.sklearn.log_model(..., registered_model_name="churn-model"), then confirm the registry now holds 2 versions. Load the registered model back with mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/churn-model/2") and score 4 new rows to mimic what Fabric's PREDICT function would do in batch.
slots.deliverable: A 2-run comparison table (C, AUC) from search_runs, confirmation that the registry holds exactly 2 versions, and the 4 batch predictions returned by the reloaded model.

slots.practicalActivity: Train a logistic regression and a gradient boosting pipeline on the same churn data, log each with an inferred signature, and register both under one model name in a local MLflow registry, confirming you get versions 1 and 2 with lineage back to their runs. Load models:/churn-model/1, predict on 3 rows, then set tags stage=Prod on one version and stage=Staging on the other, reading the tags back to confirm. Separately construct (no cloud call) a Model entity object with type=MLFLOW_MODEL and tags, printing its fields.
slots.deliverable: Two registered model versions with printed lineage (which run produced each), the 3 predictions from version 1, the stage tags read back for both versions, and one locally-constructed Model entity object.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the init()/run(raw_data) scoring-script functions for the churn model, install azureml-inference-server-http locally, point AZUREML_MODEL_DIR at your saved model folder, and start the real inference server with --entry_script. Send a valid JSON request, a 2-row request, and a deliberately malformed request (missing the "data" key), and compare the generic 500 message the client sees against the real KeyError you find in the server's own log.
slots.deliverable: Captured request/response pairs for the healthy GET /, a successful POST /score, and the failed POST /score, plus the real server-log traceback for the failure that the client never saw.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a batch score.py with init() (loads the model once) and run(mini_batch) (scores a list of CSV file paths), create 5 small CSV files of customers, and write a driver that mimics the batch-transform engine by calling init() once and run() on mini-batches of 2 files at a time. Confirm you get exactly 3 run() calls and that the merged output table has one churn_risk prediction per input row, in the same row count as the input.
slots.deliverable: The 5 generated input CSV files, the merged (20-row-or-equivalent) output table with churn_risk and source_file columns, and a printed count confirming 3 mini-batch run() calls were made.

slots.practicalActivity: Implement the PSI, Jensen-Shannon distance, and KS-test drift functions, run them on a reference customer sample against a normal production week and a deliberately drifted week (spend shifted, plan mix shifted), and confirm the control week scores near zero while the drifted week crosses the 0.25 alert threshold. Then build the lesson's synthetic 6,000-row loan-approval dataset with 2 groups, train a classifier without the group column, and run Fairlearn's MetricFrame and demographic_parity_difference by group to show the model still produces unequal selection rates even though it never saw the sensitive attribute.
slots.deliverable: A drift report comparing the normal-week and drifted-week PSI/JS/KS values against the 0.25 threshold, plus a Fairlearn MetricFrame table (accuracy, recall, selection_rate by group) and the demographic parity difference you measured.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Train, Deploy and Monitor a Model on Azure

slots.practicalActivity: Generate the capstone's 5,000-row seeded synthetic Northwind Streams churn table, confirm the 35.3% churn rate, train a DummyClassifier baseline and a scaling-plus-one-hot-encoding logistic-regression pipeline, and verify you reach the kickoff's AUC >= 0.75 target (the lesson's own run hit 0.793). Write down the 5 success criteria from the kickoff and set up the churn-capstone/ repository layout (data/, src/, monitor/, docs/) exactly as specified.
slots.deliverable: Printed baseline-vs-pipeline AUC and recall numbers confirming the AUC >= 0.75 criterion is met, a written list of the 5 success criteria, and the created repository folder structure.

slots.practicalActivity: Track 3 candidate models (2 logistic-regression settings and a gradient-boosting model) against a local MLflow store with signatures and input examples, pick the winner by AUC, and register it as churn-model version 1. Write a custom scoring script with init()/run(raw_data) that follows the AZUREML_MODEL_DIR contract and returns churn-risk probabilities (not just labels), test it locally on a high-risk and a low-risk customer, and run the PSI drift check comparing a normal and a drifted simulated production week.
slots.deliverable: A 3-candidate AUC comparison with the winner registered as version 1, the custom scoring script's output for 2 test customers (risk scores, not labels), and the PSI drift numbers for the normal vs. drifted week.

slots.practicalActivity: Generate a model card by pulling the real AUC, recall, and parameters straight from your registered run via MlflowClient (never typed from memory), then compute recall and AUC by contract-type segment to find the weak spot the lesson found (far lower recall on two-year customers at a global 0.5 threshold). Try a per-segment threshold set to each segment's own churn rate and compare the resulting precision/recall trade-off, then draw the PSI-by-feature bar chart comparing a normal and drifted week and write the 5-minute presentation outline.
slots.deliverable: A data-pulled model card, a segment-by-segment recall/AUC table exposing the weak segment, a before/after per-segment-threshold trade-off comparison, the PSI-by-feature chart, and a written 5-minute presentation outline.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can train, track, register, deploy, and monitor a machine learning model end to end on Microsoft's cloud stack — Azure ML workspaces and jobs, MLflow experiment tracking and the model registry, real-time and batch endpoints, drift detection, and responsible AI checks — and can explain how the same skills carry over to Databricks and Microsoft Fabric.
